quadrant.c: QUADRANT, is an Arch which is the fourth Part of a Circle, containing degr. And often - times the space contained between a Quadrantal Ark and two Radius perpendicular one to ano - ther in the Centre of the Circle, is called a Qua - dr ant; from the Figure of which the following Instrument takes its name, which is called a Quadrant, and is a very useful and ready Instru - ment, when well made, for many Operations. The Limb of it is divided into Degrees, and as ma - ny Parts of a Degree as the bigness of the Instru - rent will bear, and this by means of a String and Plummet, ( or Label, if it be a screwed Limb ) gives you the Sun ’ s Altitude, or that of any Star or other Object above the Horizon, reckoned from that edge of the Quadrant where the Sights are not placed. In Collins Quadrant, this Limb is also divided into Time, and numbred accordingly, and then it serves very readily to find the Sun ’ s right Ascension either in Degrees or Time, and to shew the Hour of the Day there to a Minute, by his Altitude. Next to the Limb, in Gunters Qua - drant, is the Calendar of the Months placed; but in Collins ’ tis put in four little Quadrantal Arks next the Centre of the Instrument, having an Ark also of the Sun ’ s Declination fitted thereunto so that the String laid to the Day of the Month, will ftiew the Declination; or laid to the Declina - tion, will give the Day of the Month, in the Quadrantal Ark proper for that Season of the Year. Next below this, in Mr. Collins Quadrant, ( which I judge tobethebeft ) is the Projection, which is a th Part of Stofflers Afirolabe, inverted and fitted to the Latitude of London; of which those Lines which run from the Right Hand to - wards the Left are Parallels of Altitude, and those which cross them are Azimuths. In the Project - ion are drawn the two Eclipticks, with the Cha - rafters of the Signs upon them, and the two Horizons, all issuing from the fame Point; and up and down in the Projection are placed such semi - next fixed Stars, as are between the Tropicks. Next below the Projection is the Quadrat and Line of Shadows, being only a Line of Natural Tan - gents to the Arks of the Limb; and by its help, the heights of Towers, Steeples, &c. may be pretty exactly taken.

qxjick.c: QXJICK - Silver: The Way and Manner how this strangely Fluid Mineral is gained - you have a good Account of by Dr. Pope m I'hil. Trans. N. Thus; It is found in the Mines of Friuli, a Territory be - longing to the Venetians, about a Days Journey and a half from Gcritia Northwards and at a Place called Idria, situated on a Valley of the Julian Alps. They have been for Years fub - jedt to the Emperour, and all the People speak Sclavcnian. In going thither we travel a several Hours thro ’ some of the finest Woods I everfaw full of Firs, Oaks, and Beeches of an Extraordina - ry Thickness, Straitness and Height. The Town, like others in the Alp, is built all of Wood but the Church and one House, in which the Over - seer of these Mines lived. The Valley and the Moon - tains too, out of which the Mercury was dug, were of a pleasant Verdure, which they attributed to the Moisture of the Mercury. The best and greatest of their Mines we went into is medica - ted to St. Barbara as the other Mines are to other Saints. At the Beginning of the Entrance, the Way was not difficult, nor the Descent great; but in many Places you cannot stand upright j this way of go - ing down holds not long, before you descend by Perpendicular - Ladders all the way down, and the Bottom, where there are several Lanes cut out in the Mountains, is lined and propt with several great Pieces of Firr - Trees as thick as they can be fet: They dig the Mineral with Pick - Axes, sol - lowing the Veins: ’ Tis for the most part hard as a Stone, but more weighty of a Liver - Colour, or that of CrccusMetallorum. There is alio some soft Earth in which you plainly see the Mercury in lit - tle Particles. Besides this, there are often found in the Mines round Stones like Flints, of several ' Bignefles; very like those Balls of Hair, which I have seen in England taken out of the Stomachs of Oxen. There are also several Marchafites, and Stones, which seem to have Specks of Gold in them, bur on trial they fay, they can find none. Some of these Stones are very ponderous, and well impregnated with Mercury: But others are light having little or none in them. The manner of getting the Mercury is this: They take of the Earth, brought up in Buckets, and put it into a Sieve, whose bottom is made of Wires at so great a Distance, that you may put your Finger between them ’ tis carried to a stream of Running Water, and washed as long as any thing will pass through the Sieve. That Earth which passeth not, is laid aside upon an Heap that which passeth, is referred in a Hole, and is ta - ken up again, and put into a second Sieve and so on to about o or Sieves proportionably less. It often happens in the First Hole, that there is Mer - cury at the bottom; but towards the farther End, where the Intervals of the Wire are less, it ’ s found in very great Proportion. The Waste Water ifo much impregnated with Mercury, that it cureth Itches and other sordid Ulcers. The Earth laid a - side, is Pounded, and the fame Operation repeated. The fine small Earth, that remains after this, and out of which they can wash no more Mercury, is put into Iron Retorts, and the Fire forces the Mer - cury into the Receivers: The Officer unluted see - ral of them; and I observed in all that he first poured out P erf eft Mercury, and after that came a Black Dufl, which being Wetted with Water, dis - covered it self to be Mercury, as the other was. They take the Caput Mortuum and Pound it, and Renew the Operation. There are Furnaces for. this cut T this Use, each of them carrying Retorts - in all Retorts. All the Mercury got without the use of fm ?, whether by Washing or found in the Mines ( for in the Digging some, the Particles get together, so that in some places you might take up two or three Spoonfuls of pure Mercury ) is called by them Virgin Mercury, and esteemed above the reft. The Officer told me, that making an Amalgama of Gold and Virgin Mercury, and putting it to the Fire, that Mercury would carry away all the Gold with it, which Common Mercury would not do. The Engines for drawing the Water, are all mo - ved by Water, brought thither in no Chargeable Aquedufl from a Mountain Miles distant. The Water Pumpt from the bottom of the Mine, by Pumps, on a side, is contrived to Move other Wheels, for several other Purposes. The Labourers ( being always Employed ) work for a Julio a Day, which is not above or pence, and Endure not long: For although Hone stay under - ground above Hours all of them in time ( some later, some sooner ) become , i Par aly tick, and Die He slick. We saw a Man who had not been in the Mines for above half a Tear before, lo full of Mercury, that putting a piece of Brass in his Mouth, or rubbing it in his Fingers, it immediately became as White, as if he had rubbed Mercury upon it. Those also that Work upon the Backslide of Lookjng - Glasses, are very Subject to the Palfey. They convey their Wood, thus. Aboilt Miles from the Mines on the sides of Two Mountains, they cut down the Trees, and draw them into the Interjacent Valley. Higher up in the fame Val - ley they make a Lock or Dam when the Water is ready to run - over it, they open the Flood - Gates, and the Water carries all the Trees impetuously to Idria, where the Bridge is built Very strong, and at very Oblique Angles to the stream, on purpose to stop them, and throw them on shore near the Mines. Thole Mines heretofore Cost the Emperout ' or Florens Yearly but now they Cost him not above. They produced I Anno. Anno. Anno. / /. / /. / /. Ordinary Mercury. Virgin Mercury. in all . The Town of Idria in the County of Goritia and Province of Friuli, is seated low, and En - compassed with Hills on all sides. A River of the fame Name runs by it, and proves fuffici - ent upon plentiful Rains to convey down the Firr - Trees and other Wood required in the Ser - vice of the Mines: And to this End there is an Handsome Work of Piles made sloping athwart the River ( after the fame manner as I observed in Newfol in Upper Hungary, cross the River Gran ) to stop the Trees, The Entrance into these Mines is not High, or upon an Hill, but in that Town it self. The deepest part of the Mine from the Entrance, is be - tween and Fathoms. The Virgin Quick - fiver, which they call Jung - frau, is that which discovers it self without the help of Fire. Sometimes it is plainly seen in the Ore, or falls down in Drops, and sometimes Streams out in good quantity as about Seven Tears ago it ran out of the Earth at first in a Stream as small as a Thread, and afterwards as big as a Pack - thread, but ceafed in or Days. That also is accounted Virgin Quick Silver, which is separated only by Water. Plain Quicksilver they obtain by Fire out of the Ore, or out of the Cinnabar of Mercury, which they dig out of this Mine. The Ore of this Mine is of a Dark Colour, mixed with Red. The Quick - fiver Ore of this Mine ordinarily contains Half, and sometimes f of Quick - fiver. I went into the Mine by the Pit of St Agatha, and came up again by that of St. Barbara, Defend - ding and Ascending by Ladders. I Ascended at one of Staves, or Fathoms. It has been wrought Tears, about the fame space of time Vol. IL with Newfol Mine, but comes much short in time of th Silver Mine ziSchemnit and much shorter yet of the notable Lead Mines in Upper Car inthia. In a Laboratory, where the Quick - fiver is leap - rated by Fire, I saw an Heap of Retorts of Iron every one, of which costs a Crown at the Best Hand from the Iron Furnaces in Carinthia. There are Retorts, and as many Recipients, Employed together, in drawing over the Quick - fiver in Furnaces in each Furnace, of a side above, and below of each side, June., when I was there, they carried out Saumes of Quicksilver into Foreign Parts, each Same containing pound Weight, to the value of Ducats of Gold. Some of it is sent as far as Cremnit in Hungary, for the Use of the Gold Mines: And very much carried away South - ward for they are not far from the Sontius, or Lyfon o, a considerable River, which runs into the Gulf of Triefle in the AdriatickSea. In the Castle, I saw Saumes of Quick - fiver together in Barrels, the Quicksilver being first made up in Double Leather: And in another House as much Ore as can be Distilled in Tears except they have great Plenty of Rain to bring: down the Wood. The Country is well stored with stately Firs, Larches Pines Pinafers, Picea's, and that Nobly Crisped and well Grain ’ d kind of Acer, whereof Viols and Violins are made: Whereof there is also Plenty in the Country of Sahzfmrg and Car - mold Travelling sometimes in the Night, we had continually about us a great number of large Glow - worms, which put into Papers, gave a dimrn Light like Candles in Lanthorns and the Air also P was c I Q U I Was full, of Flaming Flies, affording some delight unto us. The way to this Place from Croatia I found difficult; and coming from it to Aidofchini and Croatia, I passed over Swartgenburg, or the Blacfl Mountain, from whence I descended I o Miles in a Rocky Country, and far more Stony than the Craw, or Campus lapidtfus, in Provence. In the Valley of Lancy, which runs between the Mountains of Turn, grows a Plant like the Doronicum, ( lo also called by the Inhabitants and Botanists, ) near the Boots whereof you may find Pure Quicksilver, running in small Grains like Pearls; the Juice of which Plant being expressed, and e posed to the Air of a Clear Night, there will be found as much Mercury, as there is loft of Juice.

quintalorquintan.c: QUINTAL, or Quintan, was an Old Sportive Exercise, practised usually at Weddings, and was either so dangerous or ludicrous as to be forbid often by Ecclesiastical Authority; The manner of it was thus: A Poll was erected perpendicularly in the Ground, on the Top of which wras a len - der Beam turning round on a Spindle: At one of whofeEnds was a Sloap, or flat Board; and at the other a Bag of Sand or Dirt. And the Sport was with a long Staff or wooden Launce to ride a Tilt at the Board, and to be either so skilful or lucky to escape the Blow which the Sand Bagg would be. likely to give the Runner at this Quin - tan, by the turning round of the Beam. This seems to have been the fame with that Sport called Arietum Levatio, which is frequently prohibited T CHAT, Rachetum, from the French Racheter, to redeem, was formerly used for the fame as T heft - boot, viz. the Compensation or Redemption of a Thief, Skene de verb, signs.

quinque.c: QUIN QUE - Form, the Cinque or Five Ports of the Kingdom of England, were so called formerly, by way of Eminence: They are Hajlings, Dover, Romney, Hithe, and Sandwich. There belongs to them also, two Ancient Towns, which are VEin chefler and Rye; and several other Places which are called their Adanbers; as Seaford, Feverjham f Folkjlone, c c. These had formerly, and have still, great Pri - vileges allowed them on the Account of finding the King a certain Number of Ships of War, on occasion The Numbers of which are these. Ha - slings is bound to find twenty one Ships, each carrying twenty one Men and a Boy. Romney is to find Five Ships, with Men and a Boy in each. Hithe also must find Five Ships, and in each Men and a Boy. Dover is to find Ships, in each Men and a Boy. Sandwich should find five Ships, each carrying Men and a Boy. The Ships and Boys are. The Men. The Service which the Barons of these Cinque - Ports owe the Crown, is to attend with these Ships at their own Charges for fifteen Days, and to fet out to those Places whither they are to go, and to stay as long as the King pleases, at his Charge.
